section_name: Yearlong Planning Overview — Stepping Back to the Year
content:
Episode 10 Secondary — Yearlong Curriculum Planning

The previous episode described the writing generated during a SINGLE unit — any unit — and how the writing skills TAUGHT in Writer's Craft mini-lessons are then practiced with low-stakes experiences DURING the unit, until it's time to assign a bring-it-all-together end-of-unit writing task that will be assessed for ALL of the skills — the newest ones and those previously taught. In Episode 10 we will step back further and look at how a YEAR of writing units is organized.

Now I want to look at how those individual skills may be taught and practiced THROUGHOUT a persuasive/argumentative, informative, or narrative writing unit. Regardless if you plan a one week, 2 week, or 6 week unit — the components you need to identify are the same:
1. What is the end product students will turn in?
2. What writing skills will you teach during that unit — and likely want to assess within that end product?
3. When will you teach which skills — on what days?
4. How will students practice each of the skills taught during the Writing Time?

section_name: Why Students Need Low-Stakes Practice During the Unit
content:
Episode 10 Secondary — Why Students Need Low-Stakes Practice

One reason students may not tackle the writing time motivated is because they have a lot of pressure to do this skill correctly as this will also be the end product. Beyond the pressure, they may lack the confidence to really know what to do because other than seeing you model it, they haven't had any low-stakes practice of their own. Add to that that often the end product is on a topic that is less familiar — like core knowledge or a text — and this could stall them, and they were back to a frustrating experience. That is perhaps easier just not to do.

Another facet to understand is they're not actually doing another one. They're not going to produce another whole informative writing like they will in the culminating product. Everything we do during the unit are baby steps that are individual baby steps that are taught in practice. When first trying a new skill, this is also when you can add further support for students via peers — collaborating as a group, pairs, triads, etc. Across the 2-3 days of teaching this skill, several experiences with that skill and weaning off support.

Since you helped, peers helped, and they have lots of revision, this doesn't represent their own, independent writing skills. The during-unit Writing Time tasks ARE intended to be collaborative, and peers support one another, and the teacher provides lots of feedback. The writings that were produced DURING the unit and turned in at the end of unit weren't really representative of the individual's writing skills. All the more, THIS writing shouldn't be the end-of-unit piece graded.

section_name: Practice Skills Not Products — Familiar Topics for New Skills
content:
Episode 10 Secondary — Practice Skills, Not Products

We want a new, from-scratch, what-can-you-do-on-your-own writing experience. We are not assigning WHOLE pieces on these topics. We aren't pre-writing, drafting, revising, editing, and publishing on our summer vacation or what we did over spring break. We are attempting a NEW writing SKILL with an old, familiar topic. We are trying, dabbling, experiencing SKILLS. We are not cranking out pieces.

By teaching skills and immediately asking students to apply them within the one-and-only writing for that unit, students have a minimal chance to master the skill.

Let's marry this concept with the state writing standards for persuasive, informative, and narrative. They do not identify specific products students have to create — an animal report, etc. Rather, they describe specific skills writers need to learn and ingredients they need to possess. Writing instruction is about learning this set of skills and processes to integrate specific ingredients into their own writing — now and forever.

We need to get students to the point where they can employ a wide range of skills as they compose a full piece from beginning to end in one sitting. But to get to this level of mastery, we need to provide a scaffold of "practice" tasks that zero-in on specific skills. And that will require a lot of general knowledge topics.

Episode 10 Secondary — During-Unit Writing vs. End-of-Unit Product

The secret to these Writing Time tasks being productive practice sessions is that the topic students are writing ABOUT is NOT the same one that will be the focus of the end-of-unit product they will turn in.

This is one of the biggest AHAS about teaching writing. The writing students do during the unit is not the writing they turn in at the END of the unit. Too often, teachers teach a skill and then want students to incorporate the skill into the on-going writing that they will turn in at the end of the unit. That's the mistake. That puts the emphasis on product and not the process, on THE writing and not the writer. We are building writers. We want to teach skills, give them lots of time to practice them. And that doesn't happen with students learning something just long enough to integrate it into an assignment they will turn in.

The purpose of Writing Time is for students to practice the thinking process and execution of a new writing skill MULTIPLE times. Not just one time.

Don't misunderstand — we WILL have a bigger, end-of-unit product that we WILL grade. But that's at the end of unit, when it's time to assess what they've learned, after they've had some low-stakes practice to LEARN this skill. And learn and practice the 2-3 others you will teach in this UNIT.

section_name: Using Familiar Topics to Reduce Cognitive Load During Practice
content:
Episode 10 Secondary — Familiar Topics for Practice

During the unit, when we are TEACHING writing skills, students need time to just try the skill. Try and fail. Try and succeed. Try it with different topics. And a key factor in kids being ABLE to try the skill is that they are trying it on a familiar topic. Something they know well, something they have background knowledge on, something that doesn't require a heavy cognitive load to recall. These tasks shouldn't depend on a student's content knowledge or comprehension level. Instead, they should allow them to practice the same skill multiple times with different familiar topics.

We want them to be able to experience the skills several times, as we know everyone gets better at it through additional practice. The power in these Writing Time tasks being about everyday, familiar topics is that they aren't limited by what they can recall from previous conversations, have written in their notes, or comprehended from reading. They can JUST focus on the writing skill using a very common-knowledge topic.

Writing Time topics should be related to their everyday school life — lunch, recess, PE, passing periods, bus riding, homework, friendship, and other everyday topics. Even though I recently taught the 3 branches of government, I wouldn't be using that for a Writing Time topic too quickly. I just want to keep the MAIN thing the MAIN thing — and that is to practice a certain writing skill they just learned. And to practice it, they need to know the topic WELL!

section_name: Gradual Release — Writing Time Must Parallel the Mini-Lesson
content:
Episode 10 Secondary — Gradual Release and Parallel Writing Tasks

Let's say you want to teach paragraphing, specifically how to DEVELOP an idea — how to not just mention something and move on, but add 3 or more "legs" to the topic sentence to hold it up. So you explain the table analogy, your I Do model demonstrates this on a topic. Then you engage the kids through the same process during the We Do about another topic. Thus, the You Do task will be the same thing, just on a different topic. And have SEVERAL topics ready, because when they finished developing 1 idea, they will move onto a second and third idea. None of these individual paragraphs is going anywhere. We aren't going to revise, edit, and publish these. These are only small-dose practices so they can start to get the feel for HOW to develop an idea into a paragraph.

If we taught students how to write a thesis statement, including the components to include and how to represent the main idea — then I'd describe a hypothetical topic that I want them to try and put into a thesis statement. When they finish that, I'd give them another hypothetical topic and have them attempt to write a thesis statement for it. And then again and again. You get good at writing a thesis statement by writing LOTS of them.

Thus writing-time tasks are focused and typically just a list or a few sentences, a paragraph. These are quickwrites, partial pieces, dabblings. In fact, students are producing the amount of writing that you did in your I Do and We Do models DURING the mini-lesson. By doing that, we ARE following the principles of gradual release. The You Do writing task has to be parallel to the I Do and We Do models that occurred in the mini-lesson.
skill_title: Writing Time Must Parallel the Mini-Lesson

section_name: Multiple Practice Opportunities — Process Over Product
content:
Episode 10 Secondary — Multiple Practice Opportunities

And this is where they realize — it's harder than it looked in the teacher's model. Watching a skill is easy; doing it is different. That's why students need immediate practice, with support, reminders, and feedback. Writing time gives students a chance to try the skill right away, rather than waiting until they reach a certain part of a larger piece.

Now, the Writing Time is generally longer than the mini-lesson — and if you produced two models in the 15 min mini-lesson, it makes sense that students would do MORE THAN 1 during Writing Time. So when they finish brainstorming problems for one photograph, they grab another, and continue practicing the same skill. Same with adding precise details into their writing. If you model it with a store, and they practiced it with a restaurant, then they can practice it again with the classroom, or the school cafeteria, or the playground. My point is that the Writing Time isn't about doing one to be done. It's about attempting a new skill and developing it to do, learning to integrate it over and over, on different topics, and in different contexts, forever more.

And we want this practice to be independent — not whole-class practice, where kids can hide. And not whole-class writing generated together, because we want them to practice the skill with their own ideas and expression. Students get writing time to practice the skill on their own — right in class, where the teacher and their peers can support, remind, review, and provide feedback.

section_name: Writing About Topics vs. Texts — Semester 1 and Semester 2 Balance
content:
Episode 10 Secondary — Topics vs. Texts Balance

With that, now we need to discuss WHEN to begin having students writing about TEXTS versus just topics. Writing about topics AND texts. It's not OR — it's BOTH. I recognize that those grade levels whose state has students writing about texts on the state assessment — you would think that there is no time to waste on writing about TOPICS — we are going to focus on writing responses from text.

I recognize that in Secondary Language Arts we are reading A LOT of text in class, but when it comes to the subject matter students are to write about, there is a REASON for the AND — topics AND texts. The SHORT answer is: Typically, students struggle to accomplish the task independently, let alone execute it well.

Here's the longer explanation. When learning a new process — how to do something the first time, it's new, hard, abstract. We're all a little clumsy at it. No one feels confident, let alone "masterful." Consequently, let's not add difficulty to the task by ALSO asking them to execute that new skill with an unfamiliar topic or text.

Often we have students writing about content and subject matter we have recently read. However, they are still getting their arms around THAT information. And then we throw a new writing task at them with new writing ingredients and want them to compose a piece in that new genre using their somewhat understanding of a text you recently read — ALL ON THEIR OWN.

I can likely predict a few possible outcomes:
1. You give in on the independence of the task and are pulling everyone through the process together, as a class. Telling them what to write each day and how to write it.
2. You hold firm to the all-by-yourself component of writing and have a line of students who are very unsure of how to do the task and what to write next.

And this is because BOTH the subject matter they are to write about AND the task they are to produce are new to them. They are not confident in either. They haven't worked with either of them for very long.

section_name: Writing Unit Structure — Mini-Lesson and Writing Time
content:
Episode 10 Secondary — Writing Unit Structure

When preparing a writing unit, teachers must identify the new skills to teach and assess and provide students targeted experiences to practice them. This is the type of writing that happens DURING the unit. Then, at the END of the unit, a new writing is assigned and assessed for all the skills within a single, new product.

Mini-Lesson and Writing Time: Every new writing skill taught in a mini-lesson (i.e., I do, We do) is then followed with a "workshop" writing time (i.e., You do). This is when students dabble and experiment with the one skill that was just taught and modeled in the whole-class lesson.

Each of those episodes focused on 4 foundational skills within its respective mode of writing — the ones prioritized within the LA writing standards and should guide our initial instruction. We addressed the expectations across the grade levels and lesson concepts to teach these skills to your students.

When we focus on a single writing throughout a whole unit, we mistakenly put the emphasis on the product — over the process, the writing over the writer. By only working on one writing, one topic, for the whole unit, we limit students' opportunities to practice and develop each skill.

In order for students to LEARN new skills by the end of the unit, they have to have multiple opportunities to PRACTICE them DURING the unit. They need MULTIPLE opportunities to try the new, difficult, grade level writing skill. It's with consistent practice and experience that they develop and refine that skill. The writing students do DURING the unit is to be targeted PRACTICE on the specific skill taught in that day's mini-lesson. The more they practice, the better they get. And this PRACTICE is just that — low-stakes, no pressure, ungraded attempts at a skill.

section_name: Writing Time Examples — Parallel Tasks Across Skill Types
content:
Episode 10 Secondary — Writing Time Examples of Parallel Tasks

Let's use some of the essential skills we've learned in previous episodes to describe what this would look like:

- If the mini-lesson was on a skill and you modeled how to list known details for why a CAT makes the best pet, then we did it for why a DOG makes the best pet — then that's what the students do, using 2 different everyday topics, like: Is summer break or winter break best?

- If the mini-lesson was on a skill and you modeled how to think of names, numbers, descriptions, comparisons about a store, then that's what the students will do — about a restaurant.

- If the mini-lesson was on a skill and you modeled how to think of different story problems using a photo, then that's what the students will do, during Writing Time, using DIFFERENT photographs.

When students "dabble with the skill" during writing units, they are engaging in a low-stakes activity, just for practice, and on a simple topic. Students are not trying the skill for the first time by incorporating it into the end-of-unit product.

- If you taught and modeled how to describe an object using the 5 senses, then that's what the students will do — using a different object during writing time.
- If you taught and modeled how to include adjectives before nouns when labeling a picture, then that's what the students will do — on a different topic during writing time.
- If you taught and modeled how to select appropriate transitions to use in a paragraph, then that's what the students will do — with a different paragraph during writing time.

section_name: Standards Alignment and Semester Planning — Topics Then Texts
content:
Episode 10 Secondary — Standards and Semester Planning

State standards emphasize writing in response to reading and research, encouraging students to draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support their analysis, reflection, and research. Standards aim to have students write in various genres, including literary and informational texts, to convey their understanding of different subjects and concepts. The aim is to develop students' abilities to write about a wide range of topics, subjects, and texts — writing about and supplying information about the topic, developing the ability to write about various topics with increasing complexity and depth.

Not saying we aren't writing about texts for months (because of close reading in Semester 1), but maybe we aren't writing LONG responses for a while (Semester 2 = ERR/performance tasks). We have to build their writer stamina, their writing skill base, and their bank of writing experiences.

What may be new is the direct instruction of individual writing skills and the abundant practice of those skills with general knowledge topics — all before we ask students to write about a core knowledge topic. And IF we are trying to assess comprehension and understanding of the core knowledge TOPIC and we want to assess their writing skills, then I would NOT brainstorm facts and details together.

For them to write a lot, they will need to know a lot. The importance of organizing related details, so that when they write, the reader knows what they're talking about.

section_name: Text Analysis Components for Secondary — Literary and Informational
content:
Episode 10 Secondary — Text Analysis Components

A high school student analyzing a text — whether literary or informational — might evaluate different components depending on the text type. Here's a breakdown of key facets:

Literary Text Analysis (Fiction, Poetry, Drama):
1. Theme – The central idea or message of the text.
2. Plot Structure – Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.
3. Characterization – How characters are developed through direct/indirect description, actions, dialogue, and interactions.
4. Setting – Time, place, and atmosphere, including its influence on the plot or characters.
5. Point of View – First-person, third-person limited, third-person omniscient, etc.
6. Tone and Mood – The author's attitude (tone) and the emotional effect on the reader (mood).
7. Symbolism and Motifs – Recurring objects, colors, or ideas that contribute to deeper meaning.
8. Figurative Language – Metaphors, similes, personification, hyperbole, imagery, etc.
9. Diction and Syntax – Word choice and sentence structure, influencing meaning and style.
10. Literary Devices – Irony, foreshadowing, allegory, allusion, etc.

Informational Text Analysis (Essays, Articles, Reports, Speeches):
1. Central Idea/Main Claim – The primary argument or point the author is making.
2. Supporting Evidence – Facts, statistics, examples, and expert opinions used to support claims.
3. Structure and Organization – Cause-effect, problem-solution, compare-contrast, chronological, etc.
4. Author's Purpose – To inform, persuade, entertain, or explain.
5. Tone and Bias – The author's stance and whether they present a balanced or biased perspective.
6. Rhetorical Devices – Ethos (credibility), pathos (emotion), logos (logic).
7. Word Choice and Style – How language is used to persuade or inform effectively.
8. Credibility and Reliability – Evaluating the source and the accuracy of information.
9. Graphics and Text Features – Charts, graphs, captions, bullet points, and how they enhance understanding.
10. Counterarguments and Rebuttals – How the author addresses opposing views.
